summary.text: The numerator and denominator valuations are respectively \(\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor^2\) (by counting pairs divisible by each \(p^i\)) and \(\sum_{i\ge1}S(\lfloor N/p^i\rfloor)\), where Legendre’s factorial formula gives \(S(q)=\sum_{r=1}^q r\lfloor q/r\rfloor\); the termwise bound \(S(q)\le q^2\) also proves the quotient is exact. Since \(0\le k<p\) implies \(\lfloor(np+k)/p^i\rfloor=\lfloor np/p^i\rfloor\) for every \(i\ge1\), these valuation formulas agree.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N(m)=\prod_{j=1}^m\prod_{r=1}^m \gcd(j,r),
\qquad
D(m)=\prod_{r=1}^m\left(\left\lfloor\frac mr\right\rfloor!\right)^r,
\]
so that the sequence in question is
\[
a(m)=\frac{N(m)}{D(m)}.
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer and derive an explicit formula for its valuation at any prime.

For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(x\). Define, for every nonnegative integer \(q\),
\[
S(q)=\sum_{r=1}^q r\left\lfloor\frac qr\right\rfloor.
\]
We claim that if \(m>0\), \(p\) is prime, and \(B\) is any integer such that
\[
m<p^B,
\]
then
\[
v_p(N(m))=\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2                                      \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
v_p(D(m))=\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}S\left(\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor\right).                         \tag{2}
\]

We first establish (1). Since \(j,r\ge 1\),
\[
v_p(\gcd(j,r))=\min(v_p(j),v_p(r)).
\]
Because \(j\le m<p^B\), one has \(v_p(j)<B\), and likewise \(v_p(r)<B\). Hence
\[
\min(v_p(j),v_p(r))
 =\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}{\bf 1}_{i\le v_p(j)}{\bf 1}_{i\le v_p(r)},
\]
where an indicator is \(1\) if its condition holds and \(0\) otherwise. The condition \(i\le v_p(j)\) is equivalent to \(p^i\mid j\). Therefore, using additivity of valuations on products and interchanging the finite sums,
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(N(m))
&=\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{r=1}^m v_p(\gcd(j,r))\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}
  \left(\sum_{j=1}^m {\bf 1}_{p^i\mid j}\right)
  \left(\sum_{r=1}^m {\bf 1}_{p^i\mid r}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
There are exactly \(\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor\) multiples of \(p^i\) between \(1\) and \(m\). This gives (1).

Next we prove (2). By additivity of valuations and the rule \(v_p(x^r)=r v_p(x)\),
\[
v_p(D(m))
 =\sum_{r=1}^m r\,v_p\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac mr\right\rfloor!\right).
\]
Legendre’s formula says that for every nonnegative integer \(t\),
\[
v_p(t!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{t}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Here \(t=\lfloor m/r\rfloor\le m<p^B\), so all terms with \(i\ge B\) vanish. Consequently,
\[
v_p(D(m))
 =\sum_{r=1}^m r\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}
   \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/r\rfloor}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
For positive denominators, successive integer divisions satisfy
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/r\rfloor}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{m}{rp^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor}{r}\right\rfloor.
\]
Interchanging the finite sums and putting
\[
q_i=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor,
\]
we obtain
\[
v_p(D(m))
 =\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}\sum_{r=1}^m r\left\lfloor\frac{q_i}{r}\right\rfloor.
\]
If \(r>q_i\), then \(\lfloor q_i/r\rfloor=0\). Thus the inner sum may be truncated at \(q_i\), and it is exactly \(S(q_i)\). This proves (2).

We now show that the division defining \(a(m)\) is exact. For every \(q\ge0\),
\[
S(q)\le q^2.                                                        \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, for each \(1\le r\le q\),
\[
r\left\lfloor\frac qr\right\rfloor\le q.
\]
There are \(q\) such terms, so their sum is at most \(q\cdot q=q^2\). Applying (3) to each \(q_i=\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor\) and comparing (1) with (2) gives
\[
v_p(D(m))\le v_p(N(m))
\]
for every prime \(p\). Both products are positive integers. The prime-factorization criterion for divisibility therefore implies
\[
D(m)\mid N(m).
\]
(The case \(m=0\), if needed, is immediate because both products are empty products and equal \(1\).)

It follows that \(a(m)=N(m)/D(m)\) is an integer, and valuations subtract under this exact division. Combining (1) and (2), we have the formula
\[
\boxed{
 v_p(a(m))
 =\sum_{i=1}^{B-1}
 \left[
 \left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2
 -S\left(\left\lfloor\frac{m}{p^i}\right\rfloor\right)
 \right]
}                                                               \tag{4}
\]
whenever \(m>0\) and \(m<p^B\). Equivalently, one may write this as the difference of the two corresponding sums. Inequality (3) ensures that the denominator valuation does not exceed the numerator valuation.

We now prove the required constancy. Let \(n>0\), let \(p\) be prime, and let \(k\) satisfy
\[
0\le k<p.
\]
Set
\[
x=np,\qquad y=np+k.
\]
For every integer \(i\ge1\), we claim that
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{y}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{x}{p^i}\right\rfloor.                         \tag{5}
\]
To see this, first divide by \(p\). Since \(0\le k<p\), Euclidean division gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p}\right\rfloor=n,
\qquad
\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p}\right\rfloor=n.
\]
For \(i\ge1\), divide these equal quotients a further \(i-1\) times by \(p\). More explicitly, using the identity
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{z}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor
   \frac{\lfloor z/p\rfloor}{p^{i-1}}
  \right\rfloor,
\]
we get
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{n}{p^{i-1}}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor,
\]
which proves (5).

Choose one cutoff \(B\) large enough that both \(x<p^B\) and \(y<p^B\). For example, one may take
\[
B=np+p.
\]
Indeed, \(x=np<B\), and \(y=np+k<np+p=B\). Also \(p\ge2\), and for every positive \(B\) one has \(B<2^B\le p^B\). Thus this same \(B\) is valid in formula (4) for both \(x\) and \(y\). Both arguments are positive because \(n>0\) and \(p>0\).

Applying (4) first to \(x=np\) and then to \(y=np+k\), every summand depends on the argument only through the integer
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{x}{p^i}\right\rfloor
\quad\text{or}\quad
\left\lfloor\frac{y}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
These integers agree for every \(1\le i<B\) by (5). Therefore both the square terms and the corresponding \(S\)-terms agree term by term. Hence
\[
v_p(a(np))=v_p(a(np+k)).
\]
Since this holds for every \(k\) with \(0\le k<p\), we conclude
\[
v_p(a(np))=v_p(a(np+1))=\cdots=v_p(a(np+p-1)),
\]
as claimed.
